WASHINGTON (CNN) — Sen. Barack Obama made history Tuesday by becoming the first African American to lead a major U.S. political party’s presidential ticket, an occasion he described as a pivotal point for the country.

Obama announced to his supporters that he would be the Democratic presidential nominee. CNN projected that the delegates awarded to him in Tuesday’s primaries, together with his continuing accumulation of superdelegate support, carried him beyond the required total of 2,118.

He said the evening represented both the conclusion of one historic undertaking and the start of a new effort aimed at creating a brighter future for the United States. Obama added that he could now declare himself the Democratic nominee for president. Video was available of his announcement.

The speech took place at the Xcel Energy Center in St. Paul, Minnesota. The same venue was scheduled to host the Republican National Convention in September 2008.

In New York, Sen. Hillary Clinton praised Obama and congratulated him on his campaign. However, she neither withdrew from the contest nor addressed whether she might accept the vice-presidential position. Calling the campaign a lengthy one, Clinton said she would make no decisions that night. Video of her remarks was also available.

Earlier reports had suggested that Clinton planned to concede, but her campaign insisted she was “absolutely not” ready to take that step.

Two New York legislators told CNN that, during a conference call Tuesday, Clinton indicated she was open to becoming Obama’s running mate in the November election. Video coverage discussed the possibility of a joint Obama-Clinton ticket.

According to one CNN source, Clinton told participants that she would be interested in the vice-presidential role if Obama offered it to her. One of the lawmakers said her husband, former President Bill Clinton, had privately promoted that possibility for several weeks.

Clinton’s campaign disputed that interpretation, saying the New York senator had only expressed her willingness to do whatever would best serve the Democratic Party. Her campaign also said Tuesday’s comments were consistent with statements she had been making for weeks.

Clinton said she intended to consult supporters and party officials over the following days before deciding what to do next. She also directed people to her website, asking them to offer their opinions and provide whatever assistance they could. Additional video examined her possible future options.

CNN projected Clinton as the winner of South Dakota’s primary, while Obama was expected to win Montana. Those two states held the last contests of the Democratic primary season.

Obama commended Clinton’s campaign. As he increasingly shifted his attention to the general election and a contest against presumptive Republican nominee John McCain, he had also been speaking positively about the New York senator.

Obama said Clinton had achieved a historic milestone not only as a woman who had gone further than any woman before her, but also as a leader whose determination, bravery and dedication to shared causes had motivated millions of Americans.

Moving fully into a general-election message, Obama criticized McCain and argued that the country needed to leave earlier policies behind.

He acknowledged that McCain could reasonably point to occasions when he had acted independently of the Republican Party. Obama contended, however, that such independence had not characterized McCain’s presidential bid. He added that McCain’s decision to side with President George W. Bush 95 percent of the time in the Senate during the previous year did not represent change.

Earlier Tuesday evening in Kenner, Louisiana, McCain presented himself as the candidate offering the correct kind of change. He said the nation’s course would shift significantly regardless of who won, but argued that voters faced a choice between beneficial and harmful change—and between progress and retreat.

CNN’s Candy Crowley, Jim Acosta, Suzanne Malveaux, Paul Steinhauser and Robert Yoon contributed to the report.

Obama crossed the nomination threshold after the final primaries in Montana and South Dakota and a wave of endorsements from uncommitted party leaders, according to delegate estimates.

“Tonight, I can stand before you and say that I will be the Democratic nominee for president of the United States of America,” Obama told cheering supporters in St. Paul.

“This has been a long campaign, and I will be making no decisions tonight,” she said. Clinton congratulated Obama and described his campaign as an inspiration, while asking supporters to share their views on what she should do next.

Her remarks left open questions about when she would formally suspend her campaign and whether she might consider joining Obama’s ticket as his vice presidential running mate.

Republican nominee-in-waiting Sen. John McCain also congratulated Obama on what he called a historic achievement. But the Arizona senator quickly previewed the general-election battle, arguing that Obama offered the wrong kind of change and contrasting his own experience with the Democrat’s relatively brief tenure in Washington.

Obama, 46, now turns toward a five-month contest against McCain, with the war in Iraq, the struggling economy, health care and rising energy prices expected to dominate the campaign.

The immediate challenge for Obama will be unifying a Democratic Party split by the close and often bitter primary fight. Clinton won millions of votes and retained deep support among women, working-class voters and older Democrats in key battleground states.

Obama praised Clinton’s campaign and said she had shattered barriers for women in American politics.

“Our party and our country are better off because of her,” he said.

The Democratic nominee will be formally selected at the party’s national convention in Denver in August.

# Obama Clinches Democratic Nomination, Turning From Clinton to McCain

**ST. PAUL, Minn., June 3, 2008** — Senator Barack Obama crossed the 2,118-delegate threshold Tuesday night to secure the Democratic presidential nomination, completing a primary campaign that began as an improbable challenge and ended with the first Black nominee of a major American political party.

The decisive delegates came as voters cast ballots in Montana and South Dakota, the final contests of a five-month nomination battle, while a stream of previously uncommitted party leaders announced their support for Obama. The combination gave the Illinois senator the majority needed at the Democratic National Convention and brought his historic contest with Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton to an effective, if not yet formally acknowledged, conclusion.

Speaking before a jubilant crowd at the Xcel Energy Center in St. Paul, Obama declared that the primary season had reached a turning point.

“Tonight, I can stand before you and say that I will be the Democratic nominee for president of the United States of America,” he said.

The venue itself pointed toward the next phase of the campaign: Republicans are scheduled to hold their national convention in the same arena in September. Obama used the setting to pivot quickly from Clinton to Senator John McCain, the presumptive Republican nominee, framing the general election as a choice between fundamental change and a continuation of President George W. Bush’s policies.

Clinton, addressing supporters in New York, stopped short of conceding. She praised Obama and acknowledged the significance of his achievement but said she would not make an immediate decision about the future of her campaign.

“This has been a long campaign, and I will be making no decisions tonight,” she told supporters.

The contrasting speeches left Democrats with two realities at once: Obama had secured the delegates required for nomination, but Clinton had not yet formally ended her candidacy or endorsed him.

## A nomination built delegate by delegate

Obama’s victory was less the product of a single dramatic primary than of a strategy executed across the entire Democratic calendar. Clinton won many of the largest and most politically important states, including California, New York, Ohio and Pennsylvania. She also ended the season with a victory in South Dakota. Obama, however, accumulated delegates through a broader mix of primary victories, caucus organizing and strong performances in states where he lost the popular vote but still earned a substantial share of delegates.

His campaign’s attention to the Democratic Party’s proportional allocation rules proved decisive. Unlike Republican contests in which a statewide winner could sometimes claim nearly all the delegates, Democratic rules divided most pledged delegates according to vote share, often at the congressional-district level. That made it difficult for Clinton to erase the lead Obama built in February through victories in caucus states and smaller contests.

By the time Clinton revived her campaign with wins in Ohio, Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Kentucky and Puerto Rico, the arithmetic had become unforgiving. She could win states, sometimes by wide margins, yet gain only modestly in the delegate count.

Obama’s breakthrough in Iowa on Jan. 3 established him as a credible national contender. Clinton answered with a victory in New Hampshire, and the campaign then developed into a prolonged struggle between two candidates who each represented a historic possibility: the first Black president or the first woman president.

Obama gained the upper hand after Super Tuesday by winning a succession of contests and building a pledged-delegate advantage Clinton never overcame. His victory in North Carolina on May 6, paired with Clinton’s narrow win in Indiana, reinforced the conclusion among many Democratic officials that the nomination was effectively his.

Still, the campaign continued through the final primaries, complicated by disputes over Michigan and Florida, which had held contests in violation of party scheduling rules. A Democratic National Committee panel’s decision days before the last votes to seat both delegations, but with reduced voting strength, altered the threshold for nomination to 2,118 delegates. It did not change the basic balance of the race.

On Tuesday, Obama reached that number through pledged delegates earned in the closing contests and endorsements from superdelegates—the elected officials and party leaders who had remained free to support either candidate.

## Obama praises Clinton, then targets McCain

Obama’s St. Paul speech was designed both to honor Clinton’s campaign and to begin unifying a party strained by months of competition.

He called Clinton a formidable opponent and credited her with inspiring women and girls, advocating universal health care and strengthening the Democratic Party. The tone reflected the delicate work ahead: Obama needed Clinton’s voters, donors and campaign network, while avoiding any suggestion that he was pressuring her from the race.

“Our party and our country are better off because of her,” Obama said.

But the speech’s principal target was McCain. Obama praised the Arizona senator’s military service and personal sacrifice while arguing that McCain’s policies would extend the Bush administration’s approach to Iraq, taxes, health care and energy.

The emerging Democratic argument was clear. Obama would present McCain not primarily as the independent-minded Republican who had challenged his own party in the past, but as the candidate of a third Bush term.

Obama criticized McCain’s support for maintaining a long-term American military presence in Iraq and accused him of embracing economic policies that favored corporations and wealthy taxpayers. He contrasted that with promises to end the Iraq war responsibly, expand access to health insurance, invest in renewable energy and provide tax relief to working families.

McCain had already begun making the opposite case. In remarks Tuesday in Louisiana, he portrayed Obama as inexperienced and ideologically liberal, and he sought to reclaim the language of reform. McCain argued that he, not Obama, had demonstrated a willingness to challenge Washington and work across party lines.

Thus, even before Clinton formally left the race, the general-election contest was taking shape as a battle over two competing definitions of change.

Obama’s version centered on generational transition, grass-roots mobilization and a clean break from the Bush years. McCain’s rested on experience, national security credentials and a record of independence within the Republican Party.

## Clinton leaves her intentions unresolved

At Baruch College in Manhattan, Clinton delivered a speech that sounded at times like a valedictory but contained no concession.

She thanked the voters who had supported her and emphasized the strength of her showing across the country. Her campaign continued to argue that she had received more popular votes under some methods of counting—an assertion dependent on how Michigan, where Obama’s name had not appeared on the ballot, and several caucus states were treated.

Clinton asked supporters to visit her campaign website and share their views about what she should do next. She also listed the causes that had animated her candidacy, particularly universal health care, economic opportunity and the advancement of women.

“The question is not whether we will be unified,” she said, stressing that Democrats would ultimately come together. “The question is how we will be unified.”

That formulation suggested negotiations lay ahead. Clinton had accumulated substantial campaign debt and commanded the loyalty of nearly half the Democratic electorate. She also had leverage over the terms of party unity and over whether she would seek a place on the ticket.

Speculation immediately focused on the vice presidency. Some Clinton supporters promoted what they called a “dream ticket,” arguing that the combined strength of the two candidates could unite the party and consolidate the constituencies each had mobilized.

Obama’s advisers gave no public indication that a decision had been made. Selecting Clinton could help attract white working-class voters, older Democrats, women and Latinos who had formed important parts of her coalition. But such a partnership would also raise questions about campaign control, policy differences and the role of former President Bill Clinton.

Other possible running mates were expected to receive consideration as Obama began a formal vetting process.

## A historic milestone

Obama’s nomination represented a landmark in a country where, within living memory, Black citizens had been systematically denied the right to vote. His rise came just over four decades after the assassination of the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and less than half a century after the civil-rights laws that dismantled legal segregation.

Obama, the son of a Kenyan father and a white mother from Kansas, entered national politics only a few years before his presidential bid. His keynote address at the 2004 Democratic National Convention made him a national figure, and he won election to the Senate later that year.

His presidential campaign initially trailed Clinton in endorsements, institutional support and national polling. It compensated by building an enormous online fundraising operation and organizing volunteers in states that previous Democratic candidates had often overlooked.

The campaign also survived serious setbacks. Obama faced months of controversy over incendiary remarks by his former pastor, the Rev. Jeremiah Wright. He was criticized after saying that some economically distressed voters had become bitter and clung to guns or religion. Clinton used those episodes to question his electability and to argue that she would be the stronger candidate against Republicans.

Obama nevertheless retained his delegate lead and continued drawing new superdelegate endorsements, particularly after party leaders concluded that overturning the pledged-delegate result could damage the nominee and deepen divisions within the Democratic coalition.

## The general-election map

The contest with McCain will test whether Obama can convert the expansive primary organization into a winning national coalition.

Obama’s advisers see opportunities in traditional battlegrounds such as Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin and Florida, while also hoping to compete in states that had recently leaned Republican, including Virginia, Colorado, Nevada and possibly North Carolina. His appeal among younger voters, Black voters, independents and college-educated professionals could reshape the electoral map.

But the primary also exposed vulnerabilities. Obama struggled with some white working-class voters, particularly in Appalachia, and Clinton repeatedly argued that her strength among those Democrats made her the safer general-election choice. Republicans are expected to question Obama’s experience, portray him as outside the political mainstream and make extensive use of his associations and past statements.

McCain enters the race with advantages of his own: a lengthy Senate career, a compelling biography as a former prisoner of war and a reputation for independence. Yet he must contend with an unpopular Republican president, public discontent over the Iraq war and growing anxiety about the economy.

He also faces the challenge of exciting a Republican base that has sometimes regarded him with suspicion, while Obama must repair a Democratic Party divided by one of the closest nomination battles in its history.

## From primary struggle to national campaign

Tuesday night did not provide the clean, unified ending Democratic leaders might have preferred. Obama celebrated a delegate majority in Minnesota, Clinton preserved her options in New York, and McCain began testing the arguments he will carry into the fall.

But the central fact was no longer in doubt. After 17 months of campaigning, dozens of contests and more than 35 million Democratic primary and caucus votes, Obama had secured the delegates necessary to become his party’s nominee.

The campaign now moves from a contest over Democratic constituencies to a national debate over war, the economy, health care, energy and the meaning of political change.

For Obama, the immediate task is reconciliation: honoring Clinton’s achievement, winning over her supporters and turning a closely divided primary electorate into a unified general-election coalition.

For Clinton, the question is how and when to bring her campaign to an end—and what role she will seek in the party’s future.

For McCain, the challenge is to separate himself from an unpopular Republican administration without abandoning the party whose nomination he carries.

And for the country, Tuesday marked the beginning of a general election unlike any before it: a contest between a 46-year-old first-term Black senator promising a generational transformation and a 71-year-old former prisoner of war offering experience, steadiness and his own claim to reform.
